title: Branching (Almost) Everywhere And All at Once
abstract: It is sometimes said that a reason to prefer Everettian quantum mechanics is that it allows one to avoid the kind of spooky action at a distance that is a consequence of quantum entanglement according to other approaches. There is a straightforward argument to show EQM has this virtue, however some advocates argue that this requires we see branching as a local causal process. I explain this reasoning and then show why, given the way Everettians standardly conceive of worlds and branching as emergent phenomena, branching need not be viewed as a causal process for EQM to be relativistically local. Forthcoming in Local Quantum Mechanics, OUP 2026.
summary: This paper tackles the foundational conflict between the Many-Worlds Interpretation (MWI) and special relativity by analyzing the concept of quantum branching. The author argues against viewing branching as a local, causal process, proposing instead a global branching view. This global view is shown to be compatible with relativity because the physical mechanism does not require superluminal action across spacetime.
main_problem: The paper addresses the conflict between the Many-Worlds Interpretation (MWI) of quantum mechanics and the principle of relativistic locality, specifically regarding the nature of 'spooky action at a distance' during quantum branching.
main_result: The author argues that the global branching view of MWI is compatible with special relativity because the physical mechanism involves no intrinsic, superluminal change at a distant location, unlike the local causal branching view.
method: The analysis involves comparing different conceptualizations of quantum measurement outcomes (collapse vs. MWI) and developing a linguistic/ontological distinction between the physical process of decoherence and the emergent concept of global branching.
model_or_system: The discussion centers on the Many-Worlds Interpretation (MWI) applied to standard quantum measurements, using the EPR setup as a primary diagnostic tool to test locality constraints.
key_observables: The reduced density matrix of a distant particle (Bob's particle) is used to diagnose non-local effects; the concept of 'branching' itself is the key diagnostic.
important_parameters: The speed of light (c) and the requirement of relativistic locality are central constraints. The distinction between local vs. global branching is the primary parameter space explored.
main_assumptions: The argument relies on distinguishing between decoherence (a microphysical process) and branching (an emergent ontology), and assumes that intrinsic physical features are best captured by reduced density matrices.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the conflict between MWI and locality, then critically evaluating the 'local branching view' (which attempts to preserve causality), and finally advocating for a 'global branching view' that reconciles MWI with special relativity by redefining the nature of the branching event.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant for theoretical physicists working on open quantum systems and quantum foundations, as it tackles the fundamental interpretation of measurement and the relationship between quantum formalism (decoherence) and physical reality (branching).
